For me, when I need to get things done I just use TTY1 and Tmux. When I was a developer for a distro that happened much more, but lately I just stick to Fluxbox. But, I never thought it was bad, I actually prefer it. I don't use social media (unless you count this as social media), I don't really watch videos or look at pictures on the computer running Linux, so really it's no change lol. I use the terminal emulator for everything already, I don't even think I have a gui file manager installed on here right now. But, it's way more convenient to use a window manager for me.

I don't use a Desktop, I just use the Window Manager fvwm. I've been using it for so long I have it heavily configured to suit my workflow. Every now and then I experiment with KDE and XFCE to see if I can work with them, but I'm coming to believe that they are geared to looking pretty and not to getting things done, so this year, I gave up and will just stick with fvwm.

It's a solid position. The great thing about mastering a window manager is once you have it down you don't have to worry much about breaking changes. XFCE seems to slowly be transforming into something which might get this kind of stability, well as close to this level of stability as a big "desktop environment" can get.

There's no better feeling though than firing up the old familiar window manager and not having all that flourish get in the way.

I'm in a similar situation. I moved away from desktop environments, and am I'm currently using AwesomeWM. The vast majority of my interactions with the computer still happen via the keyboard, but I can still use the rare graphical program when I need to.

The only people I've come across who didn't use a desktop at all also had a second machine running Windows. They would talk about how rubbish Windows was and how developing on Linux was much better, and how they where "Linux guys", but then be completely dependent on Windows for anything that wasn't developing. Their excuse was always "Linux is not ready for the desktop", but what they really meant was their hacked up Gentoo distro wasn't ready for the desktop. It did have XFCE, my desktop of choice, but so minimal and primitive it was only just usable. Then they would use it as an example to show Linux wasn't ready for the desktop!

Their problem was partly they existed and developed in complete isolation from anyone remotely Linux. I regard developers like that as Linux tourists, not residents. You meet quite a few, but the holes in their knowledge can be staggering, because they only know the tiny bit they work in.

When developing on a embedded machine, I tend to have it headless and be ssh'ing in. But I'm doing that, from a Linux desktop. I always work cross platform, and often am doing a lot of the work on the Linux desktop, and then just compiling and testing on the embedded machine at key points. Because of the slow speed of compiling on embedded devices, and the mess of cross compiling with gcc on Windows, I've seen Linux tourists have a headless Linux VM to do the cross compiling. So they are affectively developing on three machines. One to run (embedded), one to build (Linux VM), and one to live in (Windows).

The command line is amazing, but there is quite a lot of things that are just better in a desktop and trying to do them on the command line falls under crazy. It looks impressive, but when you really look, you see they are working much harder than someone in a GUI. But everyone draws that line differently, but you know it when you see it.

There was a period back in the late 1990s when I wrecked my X config file and couldn't start X. This was before Xorg, and in the days when you had to hand configure your XF86Config by hand. So I tried using Linux for a time in just text mode, not starting a Window manager / GUI at all. I used the 6 basic windows that you can switch between with Alt-F1, Alt-F2, etc, and as I was running gpm I could use the mouse and cut and paste between the windows. Midnight Commander for file management, Vim for editing, mutt for email, links and lynx for browsing, LaTeX for word processing. It was okay, but it wasn't efficient. I used it like that for a couple of weeks. In the end, I built a new XF86Config and got it working again, was able to X working and run fvwm again.

My first foray into linux was Debian, minimal, so tty1. While chatting about vpn's with the roommate at the time a bet came about on who could set up the better vpn service to the house. I wagered Linux was the way to go (only passingly familiar with Linux back then and going on scant recollection of the better networking stack) and he stuck to the Windows camp. The next day he came back touting {sigh} hamachi. I spent a day getting comfy with the command line and another day familiarizing myself with openvpn. Needless to say I won the bet. The whole experience prompted me to ditch Windows altogether and move over to Linux for work and play.
